The last bus left Bellwether on a Thursday, carrying three passengers, a box of blood samples, and a woman who had mistaken it for the bus to somewhere else.

Arthur watched from the shelter outside the post office.

The driver opened his window.

“You know this is the last one?”

“I read the notice.”

“Just checking.”

The driver seemed reluctant to close the window. He had driven this route for seventeen years, and Arthur had spent fourteen of them saying good morning without ever getting on.

“Where did you want to go?” the driver asked.

Arthur looked up the road.

“Nowhere today.”

The bus pulled away. Its destination sign said COUNTY HOSPITAL, though it would become NOT IN SERVICE before it reached the roundabout.

Arthur sat down.

At eleven, a council van arrived. Two men got out with a ladder and a socket wrench.

“Sorry,” the younger one said. “We need the bench.”

Arthur stood.

The men unbolted it from the concrete. Underneath lay a bottle cap, six cigarette ends, and a penny so green it looked grown rather than minted.

“What about the shelter?” Arthur asked.

“Next week.”

The van drove away with the bench sticking out of its rear doors.

Arthur remained standing for a while.

Then he went home.

***

His daughter called that evening.

“Well,” she said, “perhaps now you’ll stop doing that.”

“Doing what?”

“Dad.”

He could hear her washing something. A plate, probably. She always called while performing another task, as though conversation needed an alibi.

“It was a perfectly good bench,” he said.

“You have chairs.”

“Not there.”

She turned off the tap.

“Are you taking your tablets?”

“Yes.”

“All of them?”

“The entertaining ones.”

“Dad.”

After the call, he went into the shed.

There were things in it that had outlasted their purposes: a lawnmower for a lawn he had paved, bicycle wheels from his daughter’s childhood, three tins of paint described on their lids as almond, though none resembled anything edible.

Against the wall stood the headboard of his old bed.

He carried it into the garden.

***

By Saturday, Arthur had built a bench.

It was not elegant. One arm was longer than the other. The seat consisted of boards salvaged from a wardrobe, and along its back remained the shallow wooden sunrise his wife had chosen when they bought the bed.

He painted it blue.

On Sunday morning, he loaded it onto a borrowed trolley and pushed it through town.

Outside the post office, he set it beneath the shelter.

Then he sat.

At half past nine, Mrs. Vale arrived with two shopping bags.

“I thought they’d taken that.”

“They did.”

She inspected the sunrise.

“This one’s nicer.”

“It’s crooked.”

“So am I.”

She sat beside him.

For several minutes they watched a man across the road attempt to reverse a trailer into a space smaller than the trailer.

“Do you think he knows?” Mrs. Vale asked.

“He’s beginning to suspect.”

She stayed twenty minutes.

***

On Monday, someone left a paperback on the bench.

On Tuesday, it rained, and a courier ate his lunch beneath the shelter.

On Wednesday, Arthur found a note taped to the glass.

**THIS IS NOT AN OFFICIAL COUNCIL BENCH.**

He considered this accurate, if unhelpful.

Below it, someone had written:

**WE HAD OUR DOUBTS.**

By Friday, there were three paperbacks, a pair of gloves, and a jar containing dog biscuits. People stopped to examine them, then stayed to talk. Arthur learned that the chemist’s assistant was leaving to train as a paramedic. He learned that Mrs. Vale disliked her own name and had once been called Kit.

He learned that the courier was named Daniel and had a son who could identify fourteen kinds of dinosaur but refused to acknowledge the existence of cabbage.

“You never went anywhere,” Kit said one morning. “On the bus, I mean.”

“No.”

“Why?”

Arthur rubbed a flake of blue paint from his thumb.

“My wife used to catch it.”

Kit waited.

“To the hospital. Tuesdays and Thursdays. I walked down with her.”

“And afterward?”

“Afterward I still came down.”

Across the road, the butcher raised his blind. A sparrow landed on the bus-stop sign and found nothing to eat.

“How long?” Kit asked.

“Fourteen years.”

She nodded.

Then she said, “This arm is definitely longer.”

“I know.”

***

The council officer arrived the following Thursday.

She wore a yellow coat and carried a tablet.

Arthur stood to let her inspect the bench.

“It hasn’t been approved,” she said.

“No.”

“There are liability concerns.”

“It’s very low.”

“That’s not quite the point.”

She pressed several things on her tablet. Behind her, Daniel waited with a sandwich in one hand.

“Also, the shelter is scheduled for removal.”

“Must it be?”

“There’s no bus.”

Arthur looked at the paperbacks, the biscuit jar, the dry patch where Daniel stood.

“No,” he said. “There isn’t.”

The officer glanced behind her.

“Who maintains this?”

“I can.”

“You’d need to submit an application.”

“On paper?”

“Online.”

“Could it be on paper?”

She sighed, but not unkindly.

“I’ll print one.”

***

His daughter visited in October.

They walked into town together. At the shelter, Kit was explaining to a schoolboy how to propagate rosemary. Daniel’s son sat on the crooked bench, roaring softly.

A small plaque had been screwed to the glass.

**COMMUNITY SEATING  
MAINTAINED BY VOLUNTEERS**

His daughter ran her hand along the wooden sunrise.

“Is this your bed?”

“Part of it.”

She sat down.

Arthur sat beside her.

For once, she had nothing else to do.
